meaning.evidence: The facts are kept almost word for word, but the American's quoted request is changed to "I need 50 quid on pump number 1", which is no longer what an American would say.

sense.evidence: "50 quid" puts British pounds into a US example; "servos", "dosh" and "the folding stuff" fit; "identify which pump yer bloody using" turns a neutral step into an exasperated one.

authenticity.evidence: Stage-Australian interjections bolted onto the original: "Jeez Louise, due to problems with frequent "drive offs"", "at the pump, cobber", "Tell ya what, in the alternative", "Streeeewth."

register.evidence: Mostly the original's formal wording ("In the alternative, ya have to estimate how much gas ya need", "This is suitable for use by 87-octane vehicles at high elevations") with tags on top; far lighter than a level-5 retelling.

tone.evidence: The practical advice is undercut by tags that make it flippant, ending a safety warning with "Don't mix them up. Streeeewth."

flow.evidence: Jarring joins between formal text and tags: "Tell ya what, in the alternative, ya have to estimate", "Well, the American gallon is smaller".

variety.evidence: A spread of tags, but all of one kind, sentence-initial fillers: "Listen,", "Well,", "Jeez Louise,", "Tell ya what,", "So anyway,".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the Wikivoyage entry, since the original's text is mostly kept.

problems.why: Quoting what an American would say, with British currency; wrong and misleading for the traveller.

A.summary: The original with stage-Australian tags and a currency error; little real translation.

meaning.evidence: Every fact survives (New Jersey, Oregon's 50%, 3.785 litres, pay first, octane grades, 85 in the Rockies, red diesel, black and green handles). Additions hang off the original: "It used to be the other way round, like back home", "eyein' off a pie that's been in the warmer since Tuesday", "so don't go splashin' out".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "doin' a runner" for drive-offs, "whoever's on the till", "somethin' flash" for a luxury vehicle, "about 92 in European money".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Aussie mate briefing a traveller: "Reckon fillin' up'll be easy as?", "this'll do yer head in", "ya just trot back in and ask for the rest of yer dosh back. No dramas."

register.evidence: A full level-5 retelling, but with no swearing at all, under the vulgarity 2 the brief allows.

tone.evidence: Stays practical travel advice in a friendly voice, and gives the last warning its weight: "And the big one."

flow.evidence: Reads naturally aloud: "Now here's where it gets fiddly."

variety.evidence: Varied openers and slang: "Hang on a sec.", "Now here's where it gets fiddly.", "Then there's the octane", "And the big one."

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the US gas-station guide, retold for an Aussie heading over.

B.summary: The best retelling: complete, natural and lively, with only the vulgarity left unused.

meaning.evidence: All facts survive, from "at least 50% full-service pumps" to "black handle" and "green handle".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "servos", "hand over that much of the folding stuff to whoever's on the till", "Unless yer hirin' a flash car", "out in the country for farm use".

authenticity.evidence: Natural throughout: "The pump'll cut out on its own", "there's hefty fines if ya get caught".

register.evidence: Casual Aussie with modest slang and no swearing; it keeps the original's structure, so noticeably lighter than level 5, vulgarity 2.

flow.evidence: Smooth: "or if ya guessed too high ya can go back in and ask for the rest of yer dosh back".

variety.evidence: Varied enough; nothing leaned on beyond the necessary "servos".

sense.evidence: Terms fit ("cop a massive fine", "sold out in the bush"), but "the old colour code" for "traditional" hints it is no longer used.

authenticity.evidence: Natural: "Thanks to all the bloody "drive offs"", "make bloody sure you fill up with 87", "you'll cop a massive fine".

register.evidence: Swearing up to vulgarity 2 ("well and truly fucked") and casual throughout, but the slang density is moderate and the structure close to the original; a touch under level 5.

tone.evidence: Practical tone holds; the crude last line pushes a plain warning toward a laugh.

variety.evidence: Varied; "bloody" twice, "cash" twice in a sentence ("hand over that much cash", "your unused cash back").
